title: 6 Things Good Managers Do That Look Like Doing Nothing
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain opens with a project review going badly, his team leads looking at him to intervene, and his decision to stay silent for almost twenty minutes, ask one question, and let them work it out. He uses that as the template for an argument against the corporate picture of good leadership as quick answers, fast decisions, and visible hustle. His claim, drawn from more than twenty years of managing, is that the most valuable managerial acts are invisible and read from the outside as passivity. He then names six of them: letting a silence sit for ten or twenty seconds until someone works the problem out loud, throwing a question back rather than answering it, letting an engineer ship a solution you know will fail so the lesson lands, skipping most of the meetings you are invited to because your presence changes who owns the outcome, leaving one comment instead of rewriting a junior manager's deck, and staying out of a debate two colleagues already have covered. The organizing insight is that each of these transfers ownership. Filling a silence robs the team of thinking time, answering every question makes people worse at answering their own, and rewriting someone's work teaches them to stop trying. Jain frames the whole set as restraint rather than passivity, and argues restraint requires more discipline and more trust in a team than action does.
points: Jain reframes each act of restraint as a decision about ownership rather than a decision about effort, most explicitly with skipping meetings.
The silence rule is concrete about duration, ten to twenty seconds, and predicts that the unprompted answer will be the sharpest one in the room.
He argues that answering every question satisfies the manager's need to feel useful while degrading the team's ability to answer on its own.
On editing a subordinate's deck he accepts a worse document now in exchange for better documents later, since rewriting in your own voice teaches people to stop trying.
The closing move is to distinguish restraint from passivity, on the grounds that sitting on your hands takes more discipline and more trust than jumping in.
quotes: Instead, I stayed quiet for almost twenty minutes. I just listened, asked one question, and then let the team work it out.
I was not being rude or ignorant. In fact, I believe I did the hardest thing a manager can do, which is: do nothing, on purpose.
Silence isn’t empty air. It’s actually thinking time, and every time you fill it, you’re robbing your team of the thinking time that they deserve.
As leaders, answering every question makes us feel useful. But it also makes your team worse at answering on their own.
Skipping a meeting isn’t just a scheduling choice. It’s a decision about who gets to own the outcome.
When you rewrite someone else’s work in your own voice, it may feel like “helping”. But in reality, it mostly just teaches them to stop trying, since whatever they produce gets overwritten anyway.
They’re really about restraint, and we all know that restraint takes more discipline than action does.
It’s easy to “jump in”, to fill the silence or rewrite a paragraph. That’s what most managers do. But it takes discipline and, frankly, trust in your team to sit on your hands instead.
